units.text: Let's compare two failover decisions by following what the next request actually does. If CloudFront misses cache, it tries the primary load balancer. On a configured failure response, an eligible request goes to the secondary. The original request is retried against that origin; there isn't a permanent switch for all subsequent requests.

The supported methods are get, head, and OPTIONS when OPTIONS is configured for caching. POST does not fail over through this origin group. Verify the result at CloudFront rather than assuming that all methods behave the same when the primary fails.

Now follow a new connection through Global Accelerator. The client uses the same static I P addresses while the accelerator selects a healthy endpoint. If one regional load balancer is marked unhealthy and another eligible one is healthy, new connections can go to the healthy endpoint.

Compare the connection before and after the health change. Check the client's new connection and the destination Region. Don't assume the service moves an already-established connection to another Region; a client may need to reconnect.

We'll trace a third-party dataset from its provider to an authorized consumer. The provider publishes a product. Subscribing gives the consumer entitlement under the agreed terms. That entitlement lets the intended account access the product; it doesn't make the data public.

Before consuming anything, review the update cadence, permitted use and delivery method. Then confirm the entitlement belongs to the right account. The way the product is delivered determines whether you access, query or export the data.

One service can deliver different kinds of products. The provider selects the dataset type and publishes the offer. The subscription governs access, but it doesn't force every dataset through the same ingestion pipeline.

S three files or data grants give object-oriented access; an A P I product requires calls to the provider's endpoint. Redshift data sharing supports querying the shared data, while Lake Formation supports governed access to shared catalog resources. Pick the contract before writing the ingestion logic.

Now connect that subscription to analytics. Redshift can query a supported shared dataset. S three file workflows may require an explicit ingestion and refresh process. A P I data needs calls that honor the agreement. Don't design every source as if it copied a file into your own bucket.

After entitled access works, verify what an analyst can see. Apply your own catalog and data permissions separately; a subscription doesn't automatically grant every application, notebook or analyst the underlying data.

Let's trace one stream without treating the services as interchangeable. Data Streams retains incoming events so consumers can read and replay them. Managed Service for Apache Flink can compute results from those events. Firehose can buffer and deliver records to a supported destination.

Ask what must happen after a failure. A retained stream can let consumers read again while events remain available. Processor state is a separate concern. A delivery buffer is there to move batches, not to act as a retained stream with independent readers.
Follow the event as it enters Data Streams. More than one consumer can read the retained records independently. A consumer that falls behind can catch up while those records remain in retention.

A processing application can turn events into a meaningful result, then send outputs toward delivery and storage. Firehose can deliver to supported destinations such as S three. Repeating delivery and replaying the original stream are different operations; know which data you need to recover.

We'll follow records with the same partition key. That key determines the shard, which gives related records a common ordering boundary. Don't expect a single sequence across distinct shards or assume producer retry choices preserve the order you intended.

Retention governs how far consumers can look back. One application can replay retained input while another continues processing newer data. Store each application's progress independently and size retention for the recovery window you actually need.

For a predictable load you can provision shards and plan capacity. On-demand manages shard capacity for you as traffic changes. It still has scaling and quota behavior, so validate your traffic profile rather than assuming every spike will pass.

A hot partition key can overload one shard while other shards have room. Check write throttles and consumer lag, and use a partition strategy that distributes load without breaking the ordering your application needs.

Producers put records into the stream. After a transient failure, a retry must account for the possibility that some records already arrived. Consumers should recognize repeats instead of treating every delivered record as a brand-new business action.

Once the consumer completes the work, record its progress. If it fails before that checkpoint, it may read the same records again. Keep the outcome idempotent, especially if writing to another system.

When several polling consumers read a shard, they share its read throughput. A slow consumer or competition for reads can show up as lag. Before changing the producer, check both shared read pressure and the shard's write pressure.

Enhanced fanout gives each registered consumer dedicated read throughput per shard. That reduces contention among readers, but won't fix a hot key on the write side. Choose it for independent read capacity, not as a substitute for partition design.

Let's follow a record into Firehose and decide what the service promises. The configured source supplies events. The stream can batch them and invoke an optional transformation before attempting delivery.

The target configuration decides how that output is delivered. For example, Redshift uses an S three staging path, not a direct per-record database write. Check target-specific permissions and failure behavior before treating the path as complete.

Firehose manages the mechanics of ingesting, buffering and delivering to a supported target. You can transform records and optionally configure supported backups. Those are delivery settings, not a promise that you can replay the original stream through independent consumers.

Monitor delivery failures and confirm what the destination received. A backup can preserve records for a later recovery process depending on configuration. If the application needs a replay checkpoint, plan that with a retained source.

The Firehose batch invokes Lambda, and the function reports a result for each record. OK means the transformed record can proceed. Dropped means the function intentionally omitted it. Don't count an intentional filter as a failed transform.

ProcessingFailed means the transform did not succeed, and Firehose sends the unsuccessfully processed record to the S three processing-failed prefix. Separate that from an invocation timeout or throttling, where Firehose can retry the batch before treating it as failed.
